I found the article OP deceptively left unlinked: here's the archive of the Ars Technica story. And, since they don't link it, here's the actual ruling.

To sum it up: The cops detained Turner because he looked suspicious and then released him without charges; he filed suit against the two officers and a supervisor alleging this violated his fourth amendment right against unreasonable detention and arrest. The cops filed to dismiss and the district court agreed with the motion; Turner appealed and the appeals court(which is where this ruling came from), voted 2-1 to reinstate claims of unlawful arrest against the officers(the claims of unlawful detention were dismissed, as were all claims against the supervisor).
The key question for the title of the article is a quirk of statute: namely, whether filming the police at a station(not when they're out and about) is a "clearly established" right; the majority argued it was, while the dissent argued that the claim was made from generalities far beyond what the Supreme Court has accepted in the past. It also argued that the unlawful arrest never occurred(that is, that it never went past detention - the arrest was never official, but the majority argued it was de facto) and that even those claims should be dismissed.

All that said, this is a motion to dismiss and holds little weight. The actual litigation is yet to come.
